results.title: Encouragement Designs and Instrumental Variables for A/B Testing | Spotify Engineering
results.content: Most of these tests follow a standard design, where we assign users randomly to control and treatment groups, and then observe the difference in outcomes between these two groups. The core idea of an encouragement design is to assign the treatment to the entire population that we’re testing on, but randomize the encouragement to use the feature. However, we are still adding an element of randomization: for the treatment group, we might place a banner to use the new feature on the Home page, while in the control group we don’t include such an encouragement. This randomized encouragement can be used to compute a conditional average treatment effect using an instrumental variables (IV) estimator. In an ideal A/B test, we randomly assign each user to a treatment or a control group. In an A/B test with full compliance, identifies the average treatment effect (ATE), that is the causal effect of the feature on the outcome. Figure 2: In A/B tests with one-sided noncompliance, users in the “Treatment” group can select into the treatment. From a business perspective, the ITT is important because it gives an indication of the causal effect of the total product experience — it includes the combined effect for users and non-users of the feature, compared to the control group. For instance, if the ITT is 1, and 50% of users in the treatment cell were actually treated, we would estimate the causal effect for compliers to be 2. Figure 3:In encouragement designs, users in both the treatment and the control groups can select into the treatment. Encouragement designs and IV estimators can be useful tools in situations where a standard A/B test is not possible or not desirable. The upsides of an encouragement design (allowing all users access to a feature and making marketing possible) need to be balanced with the downsides (possible violations of the exclusion restriction, the limited interpretability of the LATE, and the higher requirements to reach statistical power). 3. Saying that the ITT is zero for always-takers and never-takers does not mean that these users can’t have a treatment effect in terms of *D* — it just means that the encouragement doesn’t have anything to do with changing their outcome.

results.title: Beyond intent to treat (ITT): A complier average causal effect (CACE) estimation primer - ScienceDirect
results.content: Randomized control trials (RCTs) have long been the gold standard for allowing causal inferences to be made regarding the efficacy of a treatment under investigation, but traditional RCT data analysis perspectives do not take into account a common reality: imperfect participant compliance to treatment. Recent advances in both maximum likelihood parameter estimation and mixture modeling methodology have enabled treatment effects to be estimated, in the presence of less than ideal levels of participant compliance, via a Complier Average Causal Effect (CACE) structural equation mixture model. CACE model assumptions, specification, estimation, and interpretation will all be demonstrated with simulated data generated from a randomized controlled trial of cognitive-behavioral therapy for Juvenile Fibromyalgia. First, the simulated JFM RCT data were analyzed with a longitudinal SEM intent to treat (ITT) analysis, first with no covariates (an unconditional model), then with the inclusion of age, depression, pain severity and group (a conditional model).

results.title: A/B Test Causal Pitfalls (and Fixes) | Medium
results.content: # Causal Pitfalls in A/B Tests (and Fixes). *A field-tested checklist to design, analyze, and ship experiments on platform metrics without fooling yourself.*. Most teams “win” experiments that later fail to move DAU or revenue. The reason isn’t bad statistics — it’s broken design: interference, seasonality, exposure bias, or metric drift. This guide shows the ten traps that quietly invalidate platform A/Bs and how to fix each one this week. > ***TL;DR*** *• Treat independence as a* design constraint*, not an assumption (SUTVA). > • Randomize the unit that* actually *interferes (user/cluster/time/geo). > • Use pre-period covariates for variance reduction (CUPED) only when correlation is meaningful. > • ITT primary; CACE only when IV/LATE assumptions hold. > • Use sequential inference or alpha-spending; control FDR across metric bundles. > • Pre-register triggers/metrics/segments/horizon; monitor SRM & event loss; keep a long-term holdout.*. ## On-Ramp: Who this is for. Data/ML practitioners, product analysts, and data engineers running experiments on feeds, search, notifications, pricing, or marketplaces where behavior, seasonality, and network effects break naïve A/B assumptions. **Design** (unit, interference, switchbacks), **Analysis** (CUPED, IV/CACE, sequential & FDR), **Operations** (SRM, event-loss, versioned metrics…. ## Written by Diogo Santos. Tech Lead & Sr. Data Scientist at NOS. Exploring good practices in ML with practical strategies. ## No responses yet.
